research_mode: official Home Office 2026 technical annex only; cohort, closed-period, timeliness and transferred-or-cancelled overview; no parcel result or safety score claimed

sources.name: Recorded-period cohort tracing
verified_claims: the recorded-period method links offences to outcomes over time
it follows crimes from recording to assigned outcome
the resolved share increases as cohorts mature
limitations: young cohorts are incomplete by design
cohort maturity must be retained when comparing periods

sources.name: Sexual-offence outcome lag
verified_claims: recorded-period cohorts are particularly useful for sexual offences
many sexual offences do not receive an outcome in the recording year
later cohort updates capture additional resolutions
limitations: same-year outcomes understate mature resolution for slow cases
lag evidence is not a local safety score

sources.name: Closed-investigation activity measure
verified_claims: closed-period volumes count outcomes recorded in the year regardless of offence-recording date
the view is an additional measure of police activity
it differs from linked recorded-period cohorts
limitations: closed-period volumes do not describe a single offence cohort
they must not be substituted for mature cohort rates

sources.name: Illustrative rates can exceed 100 percent
verified_claims: closed-period rates divide outcomes recorded in a year by crimes recorded in the same year
some outcomes relate to crimes recorded in earlier years
low-volume crime types can therefore produce rates above 100 percent
limitations: these are illustrative rather than true cohort rates
rates above 100 percent are not automatically data errors

sources.name: Timeliness as a qualified proxy
verified_claims: timeliness measures time from offence recording to outcome assignment
it can proxy investigation efficiency
the Home Office says it should not be considered a firm efficiency measure
limitations: timeliness includes administrative recording effects
case complexity and offence mix affect comparisons

sources.name: Outcome system-entry delay
verified_claims: a force can achieve an outcome before recording it on its system
one-to-five-day assignment measures may include administrative delay
system implementation date can differ from operational action date
limitations: record-level durations are not pure investigation time
small timing differences must not be overinterpreted

sources.name: Cannabis-warning administrative lag example
verified_claims: cannabis warnings are generally issued when the offence comes to police attention
assignment on the recording system can occur days later
timeliness therefore mixes action and administration
limitations: the example must not be generalized to all outcomes
administrative lag does not prove investigation delay

sources.name: Transferred or cancelled record scope
verified_claims: transferred or cancelled records begin as recorded offences
a later decision can transfer or cancel the record
reasons include non-occurrence error duplication jurisdiction and specified self-defence
limitations: transfer and cancellation reasons must remain separate
the category is not equivalent to acquittal or false reporting

sources.name: Unrecorded incidents excluded from cancellations
verified_claims: transferred or cancelled statistics cover records initially entered as crimes
incidents never recorded as crimes are excluded
the denominator is therefore a recorded-crime process population
limitations: the data cannot measure all decisions not to record
absence from cancellations is not evidence that an incident never occurred

sources.name: Transfer or cancellation financial-year assignment
verified_claims: a transfer or cancellation is counted in the financial year it occurs
the original offence can have been recorded in an earlier financial year
record and transfer/cancellation periods can therefore differ
limitations: financial-year counts are process-event counts rather than offence cohorts
cross-year linkage requires record-level identifiers
